Under it, smaller: *Synthesized from viable donor tissue. Single administration. Non-reversible.*

The Lull had been in the air because the air was free and could not be measured and could not be billed. It wore off. It was a soft thing, a carrying-thing, and softness was expensive to maintain. But the files said the masks were never the cure. The masks were the *triage*. And the donors — the poor, the desperate, the mothers with sick children and ninety days — the donors were not research material. They were the first batch, and the compact was how you got a population to pay for its own compliance in instalments of flesh.

"It's what comes next." She said it without heat. "You've seen what the masks did to the Row. Forty thousand people breathing through a filter with no job and no bread and no gas and nothing to hold them down. You think that was a cure? That was a wound. We have been holding this city up with a soft gas for two generations and you handed every one of them a knife and told them to cut themselves free." She tapped the desk. "Continuity is the same service, delivered properly. Once. Permanently. No vents, no masks, no withdrawal. And yes, it's built from donor tissue, and yes, the donors are the first to receive it, because the donors are already inside the system and because the tissue is theirs and because nobody is going to march for them. That's not a conspiracy, Reyes. That's *population management*. Somebody has to do the arithmetic."
"Nobody choosing, either."
"Nobody choosing," she agreed, "is the point."

She let that sit. Then she said, "You have a mask log, Reyes, and a stolen file, and a falsified form. I have your career in a drawer. I can take your card and your pension and your address, and I can have your mask reissued with a monitoring flag, and you will be a man in a gray coat standing at a gate for the rest of your life, and none of it will make a single difference to Bay Four." She set the cup down. "Or you can go back to your table and do your job, and I will forget this morning."

He told himself it was the monitoring flag, the card, the pension. That was true and it was not the reason. The reason was the woman on the cobbles with both hands pressed over her son's mouth, and the ninety days running, and the fact that if he sent this envelope the Directorate would close the program and burn the files and the Voss boy would die in a room with a wet cough and a gray mouth, and Jonah would have been right, and it would have saved nothing.

[11] The Rules Committee employs one intern. The intern is named Priya. Priya is twelve. Priya is unpaid. Priya moderates a comment section in another department — a small comment section, under a post about municipal leaf collection — and Priya's job, as far as I can reconstruct it from the org chart, which is itself a footnote, is to *absorb replies*.

[13] I want to state this plainly, since plainly is the only thing the Committee has ever asked me to stop doing: **this post is generating score as you read it.** Not after. Not if you like it. *As you read.* Your eyes are moving, the counter is moving, and there is no scroll speed slow enough to escape the accrual.

So here is where I am. I have won nothing. The experiment billed me twice and answered nothing, and the answer is *both clauses, always, forever, payable on receipt*. I have an intern, twelve years old, unpaid, being ratioed in a comment section about leaf collection, writing *"this is my least favorite word"* in the margin of a document that governs whether I get a Tuesday. And I am currently, right now, in this sentence, earning score for telling you this — which means the best thing I could do for myself is keep typing, and the best thing I could do for *you* is stop.
I am going to keep typing. I am sorry. I am not sorry. Both are binding.

Beside §1.0.3, in pencil, in handwriting I now recognize the way you recognize a cough in the next room: *"this one makes my tummy hurt."* — P. Priya is twelve. Priya has read further into this document than I have. I have decided not to think about that until the end of the post, at which point I will think about it very hard.

Latency of Intent is the delay between wanting to say a thing and saying it. The Committee's position, stated without embarrassment, is that this delay is *a service they provide* — they hold the sentence for you — and that services are billable.

One point per minute of measured delay. The first thirty minutes are free, a window the Committee calls "the courtesy window" and which I call "the amount of time it takes to reread your own comment and decide it is fine, which it is not." After thirty minutes, the meter runs. Between one hour and six, you are billed a **storage fee** of 0.4 points per hour, on the theory that your unsent sentence is occupying Committee shelf space. After six hours, storage converts to **long-term custody**, the rate for which is not published, which is how you know it is the expensive one.

You know the broad strokes. I pledged 12,000 karma against the statement "The Human Race should be open to everyone." The crowd turned. At 2:15 in the morning my phone lit up with a **margin call** — automatic, emotionally severe, and formatted like a bank notice written by someone who has never been to a bank but has heard the word "exposure." My score was seized down to the maintenance threshold. I went from 12,000 to 400 in one night, which is the largest single transfer of value in my life and it happened while I was asleep in a chair.

Karma-Backed Collateral is not limited to statements you have made. You may pledge score against statements you have **not made and may never make**. The Committee books these as *anticipated liabilities* and, because a statement not yet made is still a future event in a system that has already priced the future, they are scored at issuance. The Committee calls this **pre-default**: you are treated as having already defaulted on a sentence you have not yet written, on the grounds that the probability of you eventually writing something the crowd dislikes is, per the Committee, "one."

The Committee's own description of this ranking, which they sent me in writing and which I have read thirty times, is: **"participation without participation."** They are proud of it. They called it, in the same email, "our flagship retention product."

I opened my LoI statement expecting a page. It is four hundred and six pages. The Committee has applied both mechanics **retroactively** — back through this post, back through the ceiling fan, back through the 14 bus and the schedule and the rain, back through every ticket cycle from the ninth to the tenth and into numbers I have never seen printed before, and back, finally, to my first ever comment, which I posted at fourteen and which said, in full: "first."

After thirty minutes, the meter runs. Between one hour and six, you are billed a **storage fee** of 0.4 points per hour, on the theory that your unsent sentence is occupying Committee shelf space. After six hours, storage converts to **long-term custody**, the rate for which is not published, which is how you know it is the expensive one.

And then there is the other end. A reply typed and sent in under four seconds is billed at three times the base rate, under a heading the Committee titles **Impulsiveness (Full Flight Risk)**. Karma-Backed Collateral is not limited to statements you have made. You may pledge score against statements you have **not made and may never make**. I want to be clear about the shape of those nine hours, because I have the LoI statement in front of me and it is itemized. Hour one: I wrote "good for you." Deleted it — too aggressive. Hour nine: I wrote "haha yeah."
